title: A new heaven and earth (CCC 1042–1050)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last judgment: the king, the sheep and the goats, and everything hidden brought to light. Your line was all made plain. Did you do something kind for someone who couldn't pay you back? Today closes the week. Day one thousand eighty-five.

Here's a question a child might ask at a funeral, out loud, where adults keep quiet: what happens to everything else? The trees, the ocean, the dog, the street you grew up on. All week the Catechism has been talking about people: their callings, their sins, their deaths, their judgment. But the Creed and the Bible don't stop at people. The last pages of scripture zoom out. They talk about the sky and the ground. Today, the Catechism takes the child's question seriously.
screen: `WHAT ABOUT EVERYTHING ELSE?` → `ALL WEEK, PEOPLE.` → `THE LAST PAGES ZOOM OUT.`

segments.voice: Near the end of the Apocalypse, the Book of Revelation, John sees a vision. In the Douay-Rheims: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth." And the one on the throne says: "Behold, I make all things new." Not all new things. All things, new. That small difference is the heart of today. First, creation is waiting. Saint Paul writes to the Romans that "every creature groaneth and travaileth in pain, even till now," like a woman in labor. The whole world, he says, is waiting to be set free. The Catechism builds on that: at the end of time, it teaches, the visible universe itself will be transformed, so that the world is restored to what it was meant to be. Second, it's renewal, not replacement. Catholic teaching doesn't picture God throwing the old world away and starting over somewhere else. The Catechism says it plainly: the universe is meant to share in the glory of the risen Christ. Same world, made whole. Third, the people are part of the picture. The Catechism calls this the final unity of the human race, God dwelling with people, every tear wiped away. Fourth, the surprising part. Someone might reason that if God will renew everything anyway, there's no reason to look after the earth now. The Catechism says the opposite. Hope for a new earth, it teaches, should not weaken care for this one, but make it stronger, because what people build in love now is somehow not lost. And that's the week, looking back: a Church of many callings, sins forgiven, a soul meeting Christ, the last judgment, and now a whole creation made new. The Catechism's story keeps getting wider.
screen: `I MAKE ALL THINGS NEW.` · `EVERY CREATURE GROANETH.` · `RENEWED, NOT REPLACED.` · `HOPE THAT CARES FOR THIS EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for creation. Settle, and breathe. If you can, look out a window, or at one living thing near you: a plant, a tree, a patch of sky. Look at it for a while, the way you'd look at something you were going to keep forever. Notice its color, its shape, the way light hits it. Then choose one small way to care for some piece of creation today: water something, pick up litter, walk instead of drive, waste a little less. If you pray, you can thank God for what you see. If you don't, simply let yourself be glad it's there. The bell holds the time.
A new heaven and earth. Catholics believe that at the end of time God will renew the whole of creation, not throw it away, and that this hope calls for care of the earth now. Today's word.
screen: `A NEW HEAVEN AND EARTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: all things new. Today, do the one small thing you chose for creation, and do it slowly, like it matters. Day one thousand eighty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics profess in the Creed their hope for the life of the world to come, and Catholic teaching connects that hope with caring for the earth in the present.
